name: Isotretinoin
lead: Isotretinoin (13-cis-retinoic acid), sold under the brand name Accutane and others, is an oral retinoid related to vitamin A. It is approved for severe recalcitrant nodular acne, and dermatologists also use it for moderate acne that resists other treatment or causes scarring or psychological distress, as well as for conditions such as harlequin ichthyosis [1][2]. The US label reserves it for severe nodular acne unresponsive to conventional therapy including systemic antibiotics [3].

The 2024 American Academy of Dermatology guideline strongly recommends oral isotretinoin for acne that is severe, that causes psychosocial burden or scarring, or that fails standard oral or topical therapy [4]. Isotretinoin was patented in 1969 and approved for medical use in 1982 [1][7].

It is a potent teratogen carrying a boxed warning, and in the United States it is dispensed under the iPLEDGE risk-management program [1][3]. Common effects are dry lips, skin and eyes and sun sensitivity, and the drug label also warns about psychiatric disorders [1][3]. Reviews of prospective studies and meta-analyses describe the depression association as reassuring, while some adverse effects, such as sexual dysfunction reported to the UK regulator, have drawn regulatory notices [1][6]. It is prescription-only.

paras: The main use is persistent cystic or nodular acne. It is not indicated for prepubertal acne and is not recommended under age 12 [1]. A 2023 review notes that since FDA approval in 1982 for severe recalcitrant acne it has also been used off-label for mild to moderate acne, inflammatory conditions, genodermatoses and skin cancer, with some off-label uses successful and others ineffective [7].

Other uses described by Wikipedia include hidradenitis suppurativa, some severe rosacea, ichthyoses, keratoses in xeroderma pigmentosum, and, in Japan, pediatric neuroblastoma [1]. In oncology, isotretinoin has been part of randomized trials in high-risk neuroblastoma and in medulloblastoma [8][9][10].

Its appearance relevance is through acne and acne scarring. A network meta-analysis of randomized trials, and the JAMA acne review, describe the place of oral isotretinoin relative to topical and other oral treatments [11][12]. A network meta-analysis of 221 randomized trials compared the efficacy of pharmacological acne treatments [13].

The AAD guideline's strong recommendation reflects a systematic review with evidence grading [4]. A UK review notes that guidelines generally treat topical therapy as first line and that oral antibiotics are overprescribed, and that regulatory guidance on isotretinoin has implications for specialist prescribing and monitoring [14].

Registered clinical studies include a phase 4 study of two dosages of Roaccutane in cystic acne (91 patients), a phase 4 study of Absorica in severe recalcitrant nodular acne (201 patients), and a planned comparison of low-dose with conventional-dose oral isotretinoin (164 participants) [15][16][17].

The most common effects are dry lips (cheilitis), dry fragile skin, dry eyes and greater susceptibility to sunburn; the label notes that many adverse reactions resemble those seen with very high doses of vitamin A [1][3]. A 2022 review describes the dose-dependent mucocutaneous effects as well recognised and easily managed, especially at lower doses, and discusses laboratory monitoring. Liver and lipid monitoring is standard, and liver failure is a reported risk [1][6]. A registered study examined effects on nail plate growth, and another on smell [18][19].

The US label states that isotretinoin may cause depression, psychosis and, rarely, suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, suicide and aggressive behavior, with no established mechanism [3]. A review of prospective studies and recent meta-analyses describes the data on depression as reassuring [6]. A 2023 JAMA Dermatology meta-analysis examined suicide and psychiatric disorders among users [20].

Wikipedia reports that some effects can persist after stopping, including meibomian gland dysfunction with dry eye, decreased night vision, premature epiphyseal closure in growing people, and hyperostosis [1]. It also notes sexual side effects, erectile dysfunction and reduced libido, and a 2017 UK MHRA Drug Safety Update following an EU review that suggested a possible reduction in plasma testosterone as a plausible explanation [1]. A 2024 systematic review in Cureus catalogues side effects of isotretinoin for acne [21].

The label states there is an extremely high risk of life-threatening birth defects if pregnancy occurs during treatment, even for short periods, and that exposed fetuses cannot be reliably assessed [3]. A 1985 New England Journal of Medicine study of 154 human pregnancies with fetal exposure reported outcomes of 95 elective abortions, 26 infants without major malformations, 12 spontaneous abortions and 21 malformed infants [22]. Wikipedia reports estimates of a 20 to 35 percent risk of congenital defects with exposure, and since March 2006 US dispensing has been run through the iPLEDGE program, in which prescribers, pharmacists and patients register [1].

Isotretinoin is described as shrinking sebaceous glands and reducing sebum output, normalising follicular keratinization and having anti-inflammatory effects, likely partly through sebocyte apoptosis; Wikipedia proposes that induction of apoptosis in other cell types may underlie persistent effects [1][2]. Reviews of its off-label uses cite anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory and antineoplastic properties [7]. Registered bioavailability and bioequivalence studies of 20 mg and 40 mg capsules in fed and fasting conditions have been run in healthy volunteers [23][24][25][26]. A 1985 controlled letter in the Lancet reported isotretinoin ineffective when applied topically [27].

Acne: the 2024 AAD guideline, the 2021 JAMA review and a 2022 network meta-analysis summarise comparative effectiveness [4][11][12]. Registered dosing studies (91, 201 and a planned 164 patients) are listed above [15][16][17].
Safety: a 2022 review and a 2023 meta-analysis address depression and suicide, and a 2024 review summarises other adverse effects [6][20][21].

Cancer and other uses: a 2010 New England Journal of Medicine trial in high-risk neuroblastoma tested isotretinoin therapy together with anti-GD2 antibody, GM-CSF and interleukin-2, and a long-term follow-up was published in 2021; a randomized children's oncology trial studied carboplatin and isotretinoin in medulloblastoma; and an oral liquid formulation was tested in a small phase 1/2 neuroblastoma study of 20 patients [8][9][10][28]. A trial in 103 head-and-neck cancer patients and a three-year study in five patients with xeroderma pigmentosum examined retinoid chemoprevention [29][30].

On T Nation, isotretinoin is discussed by lifters seeking acne control during anabolic steroid use, with accounts of its use as a last resort after antibiotics and topical retinoids failed [31][32][33]. Posts also mention it in long supplement and compound lists and in recovery threads for what some members call post-Accutane syndrome [34][35]. The Wikipedia article reports that some side effects can persist after discontinuation, and says nothing about a defined syndrome by that name [1].

timeline.event: FDA approves isotretinoin for severe recalcitrant acne [7].
US dispensing moves to the iPLEDGE program [1].
NEJM publishes the COG neuroblastoma trial adding anti-GD2 immunotherapy to isotretinoin [9].
UK MHRA issues a Drug Safety Update on sexual dysfunction reports [1].
AAD guideline strongly recommends oral isotretinoin for severe or refractory acne [4].

lore.intro: Isotretinoin appears on T Nation mostly in acne discussions among lifters and in threads about perceived lasting effects after a course [31][34][35].

claims.claim: Isotretinoin is the decisive fix for stubborn acne
claims.believers: Members describe trying antibiotics and topical retinoids for years before taking Accutane, which they say got rid of their acne [32][33].
claims.experts: The AAD guideline strongly recommends it for severe, scarring or treatment-resistant acne [4].

claims.claim: Isotretinoin can cause lasting hormonal or libido problems requiring PCT-style recovery
claims.believers: A thread on 'post Accutane syndrome' seeks post-cycle-therapy advice, and another member wonders about hormonal issues after taking it [34][33].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports sexual dysfunction and a 2017 UK regulatory update that cited a possible reduction in plasma testosterone as a plausible explanation; evidence for a distinct syndrome is not established in the sources reviewed [1].

claims.believers: Public concern and discussion cite mood problems; the US label itself lists psychiatric warnings [3].
claims.experts: A 2022 review states that prospective studies and recent meta-analyses have been reassuring, and a 2023 meta-analysis examined the question [6][20].

claims.claim: Isotretinoin is safe to combine with anabolic steroids or heavy training
claims.believers: A T Nation thread quotes a member using it while on steroids and drinking [35].
claims.experts: The label directs liver and lipid monitoring and notes liver failure as a reported risk [1][3]. No trial in the cited sources tests combination with anabolic steroids.
